ourAnswer: The magnifier does not make the image subtend a bigger angle than the object at the same place; it lets the object be brought far closer than the near point while remaining in focus, and the closer object subtends a larger angle. MP = D/|u|.
keyAnswer: Even though the absolute image size is bigger than the object size, the angular size of the image is equal to the angular size of the object. The magnifier helps in the following way: without it object would be placed no closer than 25 cm; with it the object can be placed much closer. The closer object has larger angular size than the same object at 25 cm. It is in this sense that angular magnification is achieved.

ourAnswer: Yes, it decreases slightly: with the eye moved back the finite-distance image subtends a slightly smaller angle at the eye. Negligible if the image is very far away; field of view also narrows.
keyAnswer: Yes, it decreases a little because the angle subtended at the eye is then slightly less than the angle subtended at the lens. The effect is negligible if the image is at a very large distance away.

ourAnswer: Grinding a very short-focal-length lens accurately is hard, and more importantly spherical and chromatic aberration grow rapidly as f shrinks, so the image degrades faster than the magnification improves. A simple convex lens is limited to about 3; a corrected lens system raises that by roughly 10x.
keyAnswer: First, grinding lens of very small focal length is not easy. More important, if you decrease focal length, aberrations (both spherical and chromatic) become more pronounced. So, in practice, you cannot get a magnifying power of more than 3 or so with a simple convex lens. However, using an aberration corrected lens system, one can increase this limit by a factor of 10 or so.

ourAnswer: Eyepiece: m_e = 1 + D/f_e grows as f_e shrinks. Objective: m_o = 1/((|u_o|/f_o) - 1) is large only when |u_o| is just above f_o, and a microscope views a very close object, so |u_o| and hence f_o must both be small.
keyAnswer: Angular magnification of eye-piece is [(25/f_e) + 1] (f_e in cm) which increases if f_e is smaller. Further, magnification of the objective is given by v_o/|u_o| = 1/((|u_o|/f_o) - 1) which is large when |u_o| is slightly greater than f_o. The microscope is used for viewing very close object. So |u_o| is small, and so is f_o.

ourAnswer: The eye should sit at the eye-ring, the eyepiece's image of the objective, through which all rays refracted by the objective pass; too close and the eye collects less light and loses field of view. Its distance depends on the objective-eyepiece separation and is built into the instrument's design.
keyAnswer: The image of the objective in the eye-piece is known as 'eye-ring'. All the rays from the object refracted by objective go through the eye-ring. Therefore, it is an ideal position for our eyes for viewing. ... The precise location of the eye-ring naturally depends on the separation between the objective and the eye-piece. ... the ideal distance between the eyes and eye-piece is usually built-in the design of the instrument.
